# Findings catalog

31 findings. Evidence types: verified measurement (checked against NASA tables and PSI-25), author conclusion (stated by NASA authors), hypothesis (proposed, not established).

## Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II)

Independence from BASS-II: `same_experiment`. Lineage: BASS.

### F-B2-01 — Thicker PMMA sheets spread flame more slowly (descriptive)

- **Evidence type:** Verified measurement. Spread rates from Table 5.1, verified cell by cell; statistics computed by TERNARY. NASA states the same direction (p. 61, p. 63).
- **Question:** How does fuel thickness relate to opposed-flow flame spread rate over PMMA sheets in microgravity?
- **Finding:** Across 18 tests with tracked spread rates, thicker sheets had lower flame spread rates. The association holds with one value per test, so it is not an artifact of repeated flow steps.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA sheets; Flat sheets 1-5 mm thick, 1.2 or 2.2 cm wide, one- or two-sided burning
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s 2-21; o2_vol_pct 16.8-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Thickness varied together with width, sides burning and oxygen; most combinations were run once. Descriptive association only; not a measured thickness effect and not a predictive model. Spread rates carry an indicative uncertainty of about 10% (Table 5.1 vs Figure 5.2 for test M8); NASA states none.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Table 5.1, p. 57; Section 5.6, p. 61; Conclusions, p. 63); SRC-VALIDATION-2026 (Section 3)

### F-B2-02 — Within a test, spread rate fell at every flow step, so a flow effect cannot be isolated

- **Evidence type:** Verified measurement. Sequence assumed to follow listed order (shown for M8 in Figure 5.2). NASA's statement that higher flow gives higher spread (p. 61) rests on per-step oxygen estimates that are not tabulated.
- **Question:** Does opposed flow speed change flame spread rate over thick PMMA in BASS-II?
- **Finding:** In all 13 tests with more than one flow step, spread rate fell at every successive step. Flow was stepped down in 12 of them; in the one test where flow was raised (M3, 10 to 20 cm/s) spread still fell (0.029 to 0.024 mm/s). Oxygen fell 0.5-2.0 vol% during each test. Flow, elapsed time and oxygen depletion are confounded.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA sheets; Flat sheets 1-5 mm thick
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s 2-21; o2_vol_pct 16.8-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Step order inferred from the listed order. Oxygen measured only at the start and end of each test.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Table 5.1 and Figure 5.2, p. 57; Section 5.4, p. 60); SRC-VALIDATION-2026 (Section 3)

### F-B2-03 — Wider 1 mm PMMA sample spread faster than a narrower one at similar oxygen

- **Evidence type:** Verified measurement. One matched pair of tests.
- **Question:** Does sample width affect flame spread over thin PMMA sheets in microgravity?
- **Finding:** The 2.2 cm wide sample (M16, 0.106-0.144 mm/s) spread faster than the 1.2 cm sample (M7, 0.070-0.106 mm/s) at overlapping flows and similar oxygen, matching NASA's statement.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA sheets; 1 mm thick, two-sided; 2.2 cm (M16) vs 1.2 cm (M7) wide
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s 2-10; o2_vol_pct about 18.7-19.0 mid-test; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Single pair; no replicate. Flow ranges overlap only partly.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Table 5.1, p. 57; Section 5.6, p. 61)

### F-B2-04 — Cotton-fiberglass fabric quenched at 2-5 cm/s after flow reduction

- **Evidence type:** Verified measurement. Table 7.1 verified against PSI-25; quench outcomes checked against the Appendix A test log.
- **Question:** At what concurrent flow does SIBAL fabric quench in microgravity, and how does it vary with oxygen?
- **Finding:** Of 27 BASS-II fabric tests, 6 quenched after flow was reduced (final flow 2.2-5 cm/s) and 1 blew off when flow was raised to 47 cm/s; 2 attempts to 29 and 53 cm/s did not blow off. For 2.2 cm samples the quench flow rose from 2.2 to 2.8 cm/s as oxygen fell from 18.7 to 16.9 vol%.
- **Material / geometry:** SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass); Flat sheet 1.2 or 2.2 cm wide
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent; flow_cm_s 2.2-53; o2_vol_pct 16.4-20.8; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Each quench flow is the last listed flow, an upper bound on the quenching velocity. Flow display resolution is +/-0.5 cm/s, comparable to the whole 0.6 cm/s trend. T18 is logged as a brief ignition that went out, not a controlled flow-reduction quench. Six quench points are too few for a fitted boundary.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Table 7.1, p. 96; Conclusions, p. 101; flow resolution p. 66); SRC-ZHAO-2015 (pp. 5-7, Fig. 7)

### F-B2-05 — Fresh fabric samples did not ignite at 16.8% oxygen or below

- **Evidence type:** Verified measurement. Table 7.1; reused-sample failures excluded.
- **Question:** What is the lowest oxygen at which SIBAL fabric ignited and burned in BASS-II?
- **Finding:** Fresh samples failed to ignite at 16.4, 16.4 and 16.8 vol% O2; the lowest oxygen with a sustained flame on a fresh sample was 16.9 vol%.
- **Material / geometry:** SIBAL fabric; Flat sheet 2.2 cm wide
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent; flow_cm_s 4-10; o2_vol_pct 16.4-16.9; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** The 0.1 vol% gap equals the oxygen sensor resolution. Few attempts; ignition also depends on igniter heating, not only oxygen.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Table 7.1, p. 96)

### F-B2-06 — PMMA rods stayed flammable at lower oxygen in microgravity than in normal gravity

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Boundary fitted by the authors; the per-test boundary data are not in this service. PSI-25 confirms test O4 at 14.8 to 13.6 vol%.
- **Question:** What is the minimum oxygen for burning PMMA rods in microgravity, compared with the normal-gravity upward limit?
- **Finding:** The rod flammability boundary reaches a minimum of 13.5 vol% O2 at a stretch rate of 8-12 1/s, compared with an upward-spread limit of 15.4 vol% in normal gravity with 4 cm/s added flow. NASA notes this weak-flow 'Goldilocks' zone is typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA rods (clear and black); Rods 6.35, 9.525 and 12.7 mm diameter
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent and stagnation (axial); flow_cm_s 0-55; o2_vol_pct 13.6-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Normal-gravity comparison uses a different test with added forced flow. Specific to PMMA rods at 1 atm.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Section 6.1.4, pp. 68 and 76)

### F-B2-07 — Ignition failed at higher oxygen than the level a lit flame could survive

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Author analysis of ignition tests; per-test ignition times not in this service.
- **Question:** Are ignition limits and extinction limits the same for PMMA rods in microgravity?
- **Finding:** Rods would not ignite below about 14.5 vol% O2, yet flames lit at higher oxygen survived down to 13.6 vol%. Near the limit, ignition delay grew to almost ten times the igniter-on time of the NASA-STD-6001 test.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA rods; Rods 6.35-12.7 mm diameter
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent and stagnation; flow_cm_s 0-55; o2_vol_pct 13.6-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Depends on igniter design and heating time.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Section 6.1.4, p. 68; Conclusions, p. 89)

### F-B2-08 — Quenching and blowoff on PMMA rods have different mechanisms

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Observations plus a surface energy balance by the authors.
- **Question:** How do low-flow quenching and high-flow blowoff differ on PMMA rods in microgravity?
- **Finding:** At very low flow the flame shrinks to a blue hemisphere and oscillates (about 1.1 Hz) before quenching; surface radiative loss dominates. Blowoff starts with a hole in the flame sheet at the stagnation region, where heat losses are negligible. At the bottom of the flammability map the transition occurs when convective and diffusive flows are of the same order.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA rods; Rods 6.35-12.7 mm diameter
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent and stagnation; flow_cm_s 0-55; o2_vol_pct 13.6-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Mechanism inferred with a model; energy-balance terms not independently measured here.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Abstract 6.1.1, p. 64; Conclusions, pp. 89-90)

### F-B2-09 — Thin PMMA low-flow extinction velocity rises as oxygen falls and does not depend on thickness

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Experimental values tabulated by the authors in Table 2.1; the underlying tests are not individually traced here.
- **Question:** What opposed flow is needed to sustain a flame over thin PMMA film at reduced oxygen?
- **Finding:** The critical opposed-flow velocity for radiative extinction was 10 +/- 5 mm/s at 21% O2 and 30 +/- 5 mm/s at 16%, independent of film thickness, in agreement with computation and a closed-form scale analysis.
- **Material / geometry:** Thin PMMA film; Films 100-400 micrometres thick
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s below about 4; o2_vol_pct 16 and 21; pressure 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Two oxygen levels only. The report notes significant uncertainty in low-velocity flow calibration (p. 13).
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Table 2.1 and Section 2.2.8, p. 28)

### F-B2-10 — Small microgravity flames burned fuel-rich and made disproportionate CO

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Equivalence ratio and CO conclusions are the authors'. The stoichiometric slope is reproduced from PSI-25 gas readings and checked automatically.
- **Question:** How complete is combustion in BASS-II flames?
- **Finding:** Oxygen consumed tracked CO2 produced at the PMMA stoichiometric ratio; CO to CO2 ratios were about ten times those of efficient combustion; the average global equivalence ratio was 1.3 (fuel rich). Rod flames became more fuel-rich as minimum oxygen was approached. Reproduced from PSI-25: O2-consumed to CO2-produced slope 1.23 for rods and 1.20 for flat PMMA, against 1.2 for stoichiometric PMMA.
- **Material / geometry:** PMMA, SIBAL fabric; All BASS-II geometries
- **Conditions:** flow_direction mixed; flow_cm_s 0-55; o2_vol_pct 13.6-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Whole-glovebox before/after readings at 0.1 vol% resolution. Single study; hold back from cross-study claims.
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Sections 1.4-1.6, pp. 6-11; Section 6.1.6, p. 89); SRC-ICES-2015-196 (Figs. 5-8); SRC-PSI-25 (O2, CO2 and CO columns)

### F-B2-11 — Flames always went out when the fan was turned off (ISS-like air)

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Abstract-level statement.
- **Question:** Does stopping ventilation extinguish small solid-fuel flames in ISS air?
- **Finding:** In BASS-II, flames always quenched when the fan was turned off, supporting the ISS practice of stopping ventilation on fire detection. The authors warn this may not carry over to elevated-oxygen, low-pressure exploration atmospheres.
- **Material / geometry:** PMMA and SIBAL fabric; BASS-II samples
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed and concurrent; flow_cm_s reduced to 0; o2_vol_pct ISS-like air and below; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Full paper not read. Small samples in a small duct.
- **Sources:** SRC-OLSON-2019 (Abstract)

### F-B2-12 — Nomex III samples did not ignite in BASS-II

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Outcomes reported by the project scientist; conditions in PSI-25 rows F1-F4.
- **Question:** Is Nomex, used on ISS as a fire barrier, flammable in BASS-II conditions?
- **Finding:** All three Nomex III samples failed to ignite. In a separate test (F4), a wax candle ejected a droplet of wax upstream, which the report cites as the hazard of melting plastics throwing burning droplets in microgravity.
- **Material / geometry:** Nomex III (natural); Flat sample
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent; flow_cm_s 8-15; o2_vol_pct 21-22.2; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Three samples; contrasts with BASS, where Nomex III did burn at 22% O2 and 14-15 cm/s (F-B1-02).
- **Sources:** SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Section 3.1, p. 46)

### F-L18-01 — Opposed spread over PMMA rods rises then falls with flow; none below 0.6 cm/s

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Same BASS-II campaign (Fernandez-Pello rods). Per-test values are in supplementary tables not obtained.
- **Question:** How does opposed flow affect flame spread over PMMA cylinders in microgravity compared with normal gravity?
- **Finding:** In microgravity, spread rate first increased then decreased as opposed flow rose, and no spread occurred below 0.6 cm/s. Flames spread at 17% O2 in microgravity, while in normal gravity no flame could exist at 18% or below. Above about 19% O2 spread was faster in normal gravity; below it, faster in microgravity.
- **Material / geometry:** Black cast PMMA rods; Rods 6.4, 9.5 and 12.7 mm diameter
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s 0.4-8; o2_vol_pct 16-21 tested (abstract says 15-21); pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Not independent of BASS-II. Authors note test points were not collected systematically; O2 uncertainty +/-0.3%.
- **Sources:** SRC-LINK-2018 (Fig. 6a-b; Figs. 7-8)

### F-OF15-01 — Concurrent-flow PMMA rod tests mapped both blowoff and quenching limits

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Same BASS-II campaign; reported by the authors.
- **Question:** What are the concurrent-flow flammability limits of PMMA rods in microgravity?
- **Finding:** Twenty-four concurrent-flow tests obtained blowoff and quenching limits at several oxygen levels. The blowoff branch is linear in oxygen and stretch rate. The lowest test point was 13.6% O2; extrapolating the blowoff line to zero stretch gives 13.3% O2.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA rods; Rod radii 0.318, 0.476 and 0.635 cm
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent (axial, onto the rod tip); flow_cm_s 0-55; o2_vol_pct about 14-21; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Not independent of the Summary Report.
- **Sources:** SRC-OLSON-FERKUL-2015 (Abstract; Figure 4 discussion)

### F-OF15-02 — Proposed: extrapolate a normal-gravity blowoff line to zero stretch to estimate microgravity limits

- **Evidence type:** Hypothesis. Proposed test method; not validated across materials in the cited work.
- **Question:** Can a ground test conservatively estimate the microgravity oxygen limit?
- **Finding:** The authors propose that linearly extrapolating blowoff data to zero stretch could give a conservative estimate of the minimum oxygen for burning, a limit current ground methods cannot resolve.
- **Material / geometry:** PMMA rods; Rods
- **Conditions:** flow_direction axial; flow_cm_s n/a; o2_vol_pct n/a; pressure 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Demonstrated for PMMA rods only.
- **Sources:** SRC-OLSON-FERKUL-2015 (Figure 4 discussion); SRC-TM-2021-0011385 (Conclusions, p. 89)

## Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Independence from BASS-II: `same_lineage`. Lineage: BASS.

### F-B1-01 — Flames most sensitive to flow below 5 cm/s; dim blue flames can persist below 1 cm/s

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Presentation slides.
- **Question:** How sensitive are solid-fuel flames to low ventilation speeds in microgravity?
- **Finding:** Flames were especially sensitive to flow between 0 and 5 cm/s. Below 1 cm/s they became dim, blue and stable, and small acrylic flames burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. Concurrent spread rose linearly with flow; near 10 cm/s, spread was 2.55 mm/s concurrent vs 1.21 mm/s opposed; concurrent quenching occurred around 1 cm/s.
- **Material / geometry:** Thin and thick solids, PMMA; Flat samples, spheres
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed and concurrent; flow_cm_s 0-40; o2_vol_pct 17-21.5; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Same hardware and team as BASS-II.
- **Sources:** SRC-FERKUL-2013 (Summary; Results: thin fuel flame spread and extinction)

### F-B1-02 — Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn in ISS air; nitrogen did not extinguish thick PMMA

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Presentation slides; no suppression success rates given.
- **Question:** Which materials burned in BASS, and did nitrogen suppress flames?
- **Finding:** Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn at 21-22% O2 and about 15 cm/s; Nomex III did burn at 22% O2 and 14-15 cm/s. A nitrogen jet at 500 cc/min weakened but did not extinguish a PMMA sphere flame; thick fuels store heat.
- **Material / geometry:** Ultem 1000, Nomex HT90-40, Nomex III, PMMA; Flat samples and spheres
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent; flow_cm_s about 15; o2_vol_pct 21-22; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Few samples; narrower samples than ground tests.
- **Sources:** SRC-FERKUL-2013 (Material flammability results; Experiment operation)

## Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment I-III (SAFFIRE-I-III)

Independence from BASS-II: `separate_experiment_shared_team`. Lineage: Saffire.

### F-S1-01 — Large-scale fabric fire: concurrent spread faster than opposed, and slower than in small ducts

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Author-reported measurements from slides; underlying PSI tables (PSI-98, PSI-100) not reconciled here.
- **Question:** How does flame spread over a large fabric sheet in a spacecraft compare with small-duct results?
- **Finding:** Concurrent spread was 1.8 mm/s at 20 cm/s and 2.3 mm/s at 25 cm/s; opposed spread was 1.3 and 0.98 mm/s. The concurrent flame reached a limiting size instead of accelerating as in normal gravity, and spread more slowly than in earlier small-tunnel work, attributed to hot-gas flow acceleration in small ducts.
- **Material / geometry:** SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric; 94 x 40.6 cm sheet
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent and opposed; flow_cm_s 20 (I), 25 (III); o2_vol_pct ISS-like air; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Slides give conflicting burn durations. Not numerically comparable with BASS-II (different duct, scale and sample).
- **Sources:** SRC-URBAN-2018 (Slides 17, 19-20, 26, 32); SRC-URBAN-2017 (Abstract)

### F-S2-01 — Saffire II material outcomes differed by material

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Slides; PSI-99 table disagrees with NTRS for samples 2-1 and 2-6 (reported by another team, unverified).
- **Question:** Which spacecraft materials burned in large-scale Saffire II tests?
- **Finding:** Silicone samples showed no significant burn; SIBAL burned the full 29 cm at 2.1-2.6 mm/s; Nomex barely burned; PMMA burned about 10 cm over 600-900 s.
- **Material / geometry:** Silicone, SIBAL, Nomex, PMMA; 5 cm wide, 29 cm long samples
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent and opposed; flow_cm_s mostly 20; o2_vol_pct about 21.5-22.1; pressure about 1 atm
- **Limitations:** Flammability limit values not reported.
- **Sources:** SRC-URBAN-2018 (Slides 15, 32)

## Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment IV and V (SAFFIRE-IV-V)

Independence from BASS-II: `separate_experiment_shared_team`. Lineage: Saffire.

### F-S45-01 — At increased oxygen, flames survived reduced or stopped flow and could reignite

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Author observations from flight video, shown as embedded video not playable in the PDF.
- **Question:** Does reducing or stopping ventilation extinguish fires in exploration-like atmospheres?
- **Finding:** For a thin charring fuel at increased oxygen (V-2, cotton jersey; low flow for 35 s, flow off for 70 s) NASA concludes extinguishment cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions. On a bubbling polymer, the flame shrank during 65 s of reduced flow but survived a 15 s no-flow interval, and after going out below the sample for 6.4 s it reignited.
- **Material / geometry:** Cotton jersey (V-2); a PMMA sample (slide 8, test not named); Large samples, 40 cm wide
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent; flow_cm_s 20, then reduced, then 0; o2_vol_pct 25.4-26.2 (Saffire V, as executed); pressure 70.7-72.6 kPa
- **Limitations:** Few events; the PMMA test on slide 8 is not identified by number. Different atmosphere, scale and duct from BASS-II.
- **Sources:** SRC-URBAN-2021 (Slides 5, 7-8)

### F-S45-02 — Proposed: a small residual flow may sometimes extinguish better than none

- **Evidence type:** Hypothesis. Worded as 'may be useful'; one flow and radiometer trace shown.
- **Question:** Is low flow ever better than no flow for extinguishing a microgravity fire?
- **Finding:** NASA suggests that in some circumstances reducing air flow to a small value rather than stopping it may disperse fuel vapour and cool the material enough to enable extinction.
- **Material / geometry:** One-sided PMMA; Large sample
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent; flow_cm_s 5 for 300 s; o2_vol_pct Saffire IV or V atmosphere (not stated on slide); pressure not stated on slide
- **Limitations:** Single test; slide does not state the atmosphere.
- **Sources:** SRC-URBAN-2021 (Slide 9)

### F-S45-03 — Thick-fuel flames reached finite size; concurrent flames pinned to the leading edge

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Overview slide; supporting data not shown.
- **Question:** How do flames grow on thick fuels at spacecraft scale?
- **Finding:** Flames developed to nearly steady lengths in all configurations. On thick fuels in concurrent flow they did not spread but stayed pinned to the leading edge. Once a flame reached its limiting size, downstream flames were inhibited or extinguished by its oxygen 'shadow'. In one case a flame jumped a 4.5 cm gap to a previously warmed PMMA surface. Thick-fuel growth was dissimilar from NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
- **Material / geometry:** PMMA, fabrics; Large thin and thick samples
- **Conditions:** flow_direction concurrent and opposed; flow_cm_s 20; o2_vol_pct 22.0-26.2; pressure 70.7-100 kPa
- **Limitations:** Preliminary results.
- **Sources:** SRC-URBAN-2021 (Slide 13)

### F-S5-01 — Ribs accelerated opposed flame spread on PMMA, more so for narrower ribs

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Based on flame-front tracking per rib (slide 7), but the tracking plots export with no data, so no spread rates can be quoted.
- **Question:** How does surface structure affect opposed flame spread over thick PMMA?
- **Finding:** Ribs significantly accelerated the opposed spread rate, and the narrower the rib, the larger the effect. Spread along the 10 mm rib was only slightly faster than over a flat plate.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA, structured; 200 x 400 mm, 10 mm base with 3 mm ribs 1-10 mm wide on both sides (16 mm total), 2 cm between rib faces
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s 20 for 360 s, then 5 for 300 s (ZARM); o2_vol_pct 25.7 as executed (NASA); 26.9 inflow (ZARM); pressure 72.6 kPa as executed (NASA); 761 hPa (ZARM)
- **Limitations:** No numeric spread rates available. Single test. Two NASA-coauthored sources give different atmospheres.
- **Sources:** SRC-EIGENBROD-2021 (Slides 3, 5, 7, 11); SRC-URBAN-2021 (Slides 5, 12)

### F-S5-02 — Wider ribs carried more independently propagating edge flames

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Observation from video.
- **Question:** How does rib width change flame structure?
- **Finding:** Wider ribs showed increasingly independent edge flames. A flame that reached the specimen's leading edge stayed there and spread only across the edge's width.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA, structured; Ribs 1-10 mm wide
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s 20; o2_vol_pct 25.7-26.9; pressure 72.6-76.1 kPa
- **Limitations:** Single test; images only.
- **Sources:** SRC-EIGENBROD-2021 (Slide 11)

### F-S5-03 — Oxygen 'shadowing' limits flame length and extinguishes downstream flames

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Mechanistic interpretation of observed finite flame lengths; oxygen concentrations near the flame were not measured in the slides.
- **Question:** Why do microgravity flames on thick fuels reach finite lengths?
- **Finding:** Flame lengths are finite because pyrolysing material under the flame is protected by it from oxygen; flames in the shadow of other flames extinguish. NASA's overview slide reports downstream flames inhibited or extinguished by the upstream flame's oxygen shadow.
- **Material / geometry:** PMMA; Structured and flat samples
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed and concurrent; flow_cm_s 20; o2_vol_pct 22-26.9; pressure 70.7-100 kPa
- **Limitations:** Interpretation; no local oxygen measurement shown.
- **Sources:** SRC-EIGENBROD-2021 (Slide 11); SRC-URBAN-2021 (Slide 13)

### F-S5-04 — Small flow disturbances increased propagation speed and changed ignition

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Qualitative flow visualisation (slides 6, 10) plus tracking not shown in the PDF.
- **Question:** How sensitive is opposed flame spread to disturbances in the incoming flow?
- **Finding:** Flow visualisation shows the incoming flow slightly disturbed by incompletely burned remnants of the earlier cotton sample, a clearly perturbed flow field, and deviating combustion progress at ribs 8-10. The authors conclude that even small perturbations of the stratification considerably increase propagation velocity, and that the disturbance delayed ignition and produced deflagration-type ignition.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA, structured; Ribs 8-10 region
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed; flow_cm_s about 20 (inlet 19.8 shown in flow-visualisation frame); o2_vol_pct 25.7-26.9; pressure 72.6-76.1 kPa
- **Limitations:** Upstream disturbance was incidental, not controlled. No numeric velocity change reported.
- **Sources:** SRC-EIGENBROD-2021 (Slides 6, 10, 11)

### F-S5-05 — Proposed: disturbing a stratified microgravity fire during firefighting could cause a backdraft

- **Evidence type:** Hypothesis. Deduced in the conclusions; no backdraft was tested and no flue-gas quantity is reported in the slides.
- **Question:** Could active firefighting create a backdraft hazard in microgravity?
- **Finding:** The authors deduce that disturbing the stratification during active fire tackling could quickly lead to dangerous backdraft, all the more because microgravity combustion produces much larger quantities of combustible flue gases than ground fires.
- **Material / geometry:** PMMA; n/a
- **Conditions:** flow_direction n/a; flow_cm_s n/a; o2_vol_pct n/a; pressure n/a
- **Limitations:** Untested. The flue-gas comparison is asserted, not measured in this source; BASS-II fuel-rich burning (F-B2-10) is consistent but separate.
- **Sources:** SRC-EIGENBROD-2021 (Slide 11)

### F-S5-06 — Authors judge concurrent flame propagation unlikely on the structured sample

- **Evidence type:** Hypothesis. Generalization from an opposed-flow test; the basis is not explained in the slides. Consistent with NASA's slide 13 observation that thick-fuel concurrent flames stayed pinned to the leading edge.
- **Question:** Did flames spread with the flow on the structured PMMA sample?
- **Finding:** The authors state the experiment shows concurrent flame propagation is unlikely.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA, structured; Structured sample
- **Conditions:** flow_direction opposed test; flow_cm_s 20 then 5; o2_vol_pct 25.7-26.9; pressure 72.6-76.1 kPa
- **Limitations:** Scope unclear; conflicts with concurrent spread observed on thin fuels (F-S1-01).
- **Sources:** SRC-EIGENBROD-2021 (Slide 11)

## Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction - Growth and Extinction Limit (SOFIE-GEL)

Independence from BASS-II: `separate_investigation`. Lineage: SoFIE.

### F-GEL-01 — SoFIE-GEL: two quenching, two blowoff and one transitional extinction on PMMA spheres

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Author-reported case values from Table 1 of a manuscript.
- **Question:** How do quenching and blowoff differ on a thick PMMA sphere in an independent apparatus?
- **Finding:** Quenching at 4.83 cm/s (14.21% O2) and 0.44 cm/s (20.77% O2); blowoff at 34.28 cm/s (14.99%) and 49.68 cm/s (14.37%); a smooth transition at 11.50 cm/s (13.54%). In quenching the flame tip shrinks upstream and pulsates; in blowoff a hole opens at the stagnation point and the flame base pulsates. Heat loss matters for quenching but only modestly for blowoff.
- **Material / geometry:** Cast PMMA; 4 cm diameter sphere
- **Conditions:** flow_direction forced flow onto sphere; flow_cm_s 0.44-49.68 (cases); o2_vol_pct 13.54-20.77 at extinction; pressure 1.03-1.07 atm
- **Limitations:** Five cases; manuscript version. Sphere geometry; not numerically comparable with BASS-II rods or fabric.
- **Sources:** SRC-GEL-2024 (Table 1, p. 3; pp. 3-8)

## Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)

Independence from BASS-II: `separate_investigation`. Lineage: FLEX.

### F-FLEX-01 — FLEX catalogues 284 droplet tests without interpreting them

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Report statements.
- **Question:** What does the FLEX dataset contain and how should its outcomes be read?
- **Finding:** The report presents the first 284 tests and states it does not interpret them. A fuel-needle contaminant probably caused the disruptive endings for methanol, so 'Disruption' is not a fire outcome.
- **Material / geometry:** Methanol and n-heptane droplets; Droplets 2-5 mm
- **Conditions:** flow_direction quiescent or slow fiber translation; flow_cm_s n/a; o2_vol_pct about 12-34 mole fraction range in PSI-69; pressure 0.70-3.05 atm
- **Limitations:** Liquid droplets; not comparable with solid-fuel spread.
- **Sources:** SRC-FLEX-TP-2015 (Executive Summary, p. 1; Sections 5-6, pp. 16-17; Table IX, p. 20)

## Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R)

Independence from BASS-II: `separate_investigation`. Lineage: SAME.

### F-SAMER-01 — SAME-R: most smoke particles were 200-400 nm

- **Evidence type:** Author conclusion. Abstract only.
- **Question:** What size are smoke particles from overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity?
- **Finding:** Most average smoke particle sizes fell between 200 and 400 nm; some quiescent cases produced substantially larger particles. Intended to guide future smoke detector design.
- **Material / geometry:** Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, Pyrell; Heated samples
- **Conditions:** flow_direction n/a; flow_cm_s 0-8.1; o2_vol_pct cabin air; pressure cabin
- **Limitations:** Non-flaming; abstract-level.
- **Sources:** SRC-SAMER-2012 (Abstract)
